stories.headline: Update: Speaker Mike Johnson Will Not Seek Minority Leader Post After House GOP Defeat
stories.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told staff on a Wednesday morning call that he will not run for Republican leader in the next Congress, according to multiple sources. The decision comes a day after Democrats won control of the House and, with it, a sweep of both chambers. Johnson led the House GOP through one of the slimmest majorities in modern times and had grown close to President Trump.

His exit opens a contest among House Republicans, who are days from choosing their new leaders. Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is expected to announce a bid for minority leader, his second attempt at the top House Republican job, and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, has been floated as a possible rival. Asked about the race, Trump said, "We'll stay out of it," and called Johnson "fantastic." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., expected to become speaker, said Democrats would focus on affordability and indicated they expect at least 255 seats.

The fallout extended beyond the House. Trump said the Iran war was the "primary reason" for the losses but that he would have launched it anyway, and he maintained that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot. Vice President JD Vance wrote on social media that "the reason we lost is the war," a sign of distance from the president. Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney cited tariffs, the war and other policies, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the results close to an "extinction-level event." Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans would work with Trump against "Democrat extremism."

Democrats are already signaling oversight plans, including subpoenas and document-preservation letters to agencies, and Trump said he is not worried about impeachment, arguing it would destroy the Democratic party. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said he expects to be re-elected leader despite opposition from some newly elected senators, and pledged to use the power of the purse to push to end the Iran war. Markets rose on expectations of gridlock, and oil prices fell about $8 a barrel on hopes of an off-ramp from the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Releases Bodycam Video of Russian 'Double-Tap' Glide Bomb Attack That Killed at Least 40
stories.summary:
Ukraine's national police released bodycam footage on Wednesday that they say shows the moments between two powerful Russian bomb strikes on the southern village of Kamyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region. The video, taken from a camera on one of the police officers killed, shows residents walking into an underground shelter after the first attack on Monday. Seconds later a blast is heard, flames are seen and the recording stops. BBC Verify confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the state emergencies service showing the aftermath.

Ukraine says nine glide bombs, some weighing 3,000 kilograms, hit the village as people gathered at a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid. The death toll now stands at at least 40. President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, with the search operation entering its third day.

Zelensky said the Russians first struck people who had come to receive aid, and then the rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene. He described the attack as one of "thousands" of Russian war crimes and said there had been "very little reaction from the world." The Russian military has not publicly commented on the strike.

The new development is the release of the video evidence and the rising toll, which adds detail to earlier reports of the deadly Russian strikes on Ukrainian civilians. The attack came as fighting returned to the Kherson region after the longest ceasefire of the war.

stories.headline: Update: French Blood Storage Hit by Freezer Hacks as Experts Debate Culprits
stories.summary:
French authorities say refrigeration units used by medical facilities to store blood for donations were affected by the recent wave of cyber-attacks on European cold storage. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms were targeted and temperatures were set to rise, but staff intervened to protect supplies. It said no health impact has been identified and no blood products were lost. Until now, only supermarkets were known to have been affected.

Online rumors have linked the attacks to Russian hacktivist groups Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, which claimed to have hacked Danfoss, a maker of the systems involved. Analysts now question whether that makes them responsible for the supermarket attacks. Experts say Iranian hacktivists, nation-state hackers or even teenagers pulling pranks cannot be ruled out.

Three cyber-security firms have deployed decoy freezer software, known as honeypots, to study how attackers operate. Ryan Dewhurst of Spanish firm Previdian said the simultaneous hits suggest planning and coordination. He noted the devices were poorly protected and the known attack methods were easy to exploit, yet the attackers still had to compile a target list of public IP addresses and choose timing. Temperature increases appear to have happened overnight for maximum damage.

The new development is the discovery that medical blood storage was affected, widening the scope of an incident previously confined to supermarkets across seven European countries. Investigators continue to analyze evidence to identify those responsible.

stories.headline: Canada and China Extend Agricultural Tariff Deal Through 2028
stories.summary:
Canada and China have extended an agreement lowering Beijing's agricultural tariffs on Canadian goods through the end of 2028. The two governments also pledged to continue discussions on boosting Canadian exports to China.

The extension provides continued market access for Canadian farm exporters and gives producers several more years of tariff certainty. Details of the specific products covered and the tariff levels were not included in the initial report.

The move comes as Canada pursues trade talks on multiple fronts, including negotiations with the United States, where Prime Minister Mark Carney has reported progress.

stories.headline: Hungary Opens Communist-Era Secret Police Files to the Public
stories.summary:
Hungary on Wednesday opened communist-era secret police files to the public, 37 years after the fall of communism. Prime Minister Peter Magyar announced the move at the state archives in Budapest, saying it would help Hungarian society heal from 45 years of communist rule. The date is symbolic: on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks entered Budapest to crush the Hungarian revolution.

The names and personal data of about 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services are now available on a government website. Entries typically list the informer's real name, codename, date of birth, address, motive for recruitment and handling officer. Another batch, the "B-dossiers," offering more detail on recruitment, is being digitized and will be released on 25 February. An estimated 150,000 to 160,000 people were recruited as informers between 1944 and 1990.

Magyar, whose pledge to open the files was central to his landslide victory in April, asked everyone to treat the documents "with dignity and humanity." He warned that many families will face difficult information, often about deceased relatives. Critics say the move comes too late, that the files are incomplete because many were shredded or withheld, and that it risks division and anguish. They note that many informers were blackmailed or coerced, and fear people will judge too quickly.

stories.headline: Update: Election Day Voter Poll Shows Economy and Democracy as Top Issues, Majority Say Trump Policies Hurt Economy
stories.summary:
An election day Voter Poll conducted by SSRS for a consortium of news organizations found that the economy and the state of democracy were the top concerns of US voters in the 2026 midterms. Of more than 79,000 respondents, 39% named the economy as the most important issue and 32% named the state of democracy. Immigration was the top issue for 14%, while healthcare, foreign policy and crime ranked first for smaller shares. The figures are estimates and may be updated as more data arrives.

Voters expressed broad pessimism about economic conditions. Some 75% described the national economy as "not so good or poor," while 25% called it excellent or good. On personal finances, 44% said their family was worse off than two years ago, 38% said about the same and 18% said better. Almost eight in 10 (79%) said inflation had caused their family moderate or severe hardship in the past year, and majorities said they were very concerned about fuel costs (59%) and food prices (58%).

On President Trump, 65% said his policies had worsened economic conditions, 27% said they had improved them and 8% said they made no difference. Asked whether the vote was a way to express a view on Trump, 43% cited opposition, 41% said he was not a factor and 16% cited support. Some 38% said they were angry about the direction of the country and 37% dissatisfied, while 18% were satisfied. A further 90% said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote.

The data adds detail to Democratic wins in the Senate and House already reported today. Republican-aligned outlets and Democratic-aligned outlets have both covered the poll, with Democrats pointing to the economic and democracy concerns as a verdict on the administration, while Republicans have emphasized that the survey captures a snapshot of sentiment that may shift as counting continues.

stories.headline: Update: Democratic Senate Wave Reaches Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine; Florida Redistricting Push Falls Short
stories.summary:
Fuller results show the Democratic gains in the Senate extending well beyond expectations. Democrats won North Carolina, a likely pickup, but also flipped South Carolina, Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine, and held Michigan. Kansas had not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. One seat in Alaska remains a toss-up, and CBS News reports Mississippi is on a knife edge.

The shift was visible nationwide. Texas moved about nine points toward Democrats compared with the 2024 Senate race. CBS News, the BBC's partner, projected a Democratic House victory just after 03:00 GMT Wednesday, and attention has turned to the size of the majority as counting continues.

In Florida, Democrats held Districts 14 and 25 and won District 22, all redrawn by Republicans so that they shifted from majority Kamala Harris voters in 2024 to majority Donald Trump voters. The results are a blow to the Republican redistricting effort in the state. The Voter Poll indicates Hispanic voters backed Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon 55% to 44% over Republican Ashley Moody, reversing an estimated 55% Hispanic vote for Trump in 2024.

The poll also indicates women turned out in large numbers and mostly voted Democratic, while men split evenly between the parties. Republicans have been defending slim majorities, and the results will reshape congressional control and the legislative agenda for the remainder of Trump's second term. Final tallies in the remaining races are still being counted.

stories.headline: Apple Beats Fourth-Quarter Estimates in First Earnings Call Under CEO John Ternus, but China Revenue Misses and Shares Fall
stories.summary:
Apple reported fourth-quarter earnings per share of $2.10 on revenue of $114.48 billion, topping Wall Street forecasts of $2.00 and $113.46 billion. A year earlier it posted EPS of $1.85 and revenue of $102.46 billion. iPhone sales reached $57.58 billion against an estimate of $56.48 billion, and Mac revenue of $10.79 billion beat expectations of $9.69 billion. Shares fell about 4% before the bell.

Greater China revenue came in at $17.54 billion, short of the $18.75 billion analysts expected, even though the company described it as up 28% year over year. Services revenue of $31.57 billion was in line with projections. It was the first earnings call for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook on Sept. 1.

The company flagged supply constraints on Mac and iPad in the December quarter, driven by memory shortages from higher-than-expected demand, and COO Sabih Khan said it is hard to predict when supply and demand for the iPhone Duo will balance. Ternus called current memory pricing "unprecedented," attributing the surge to the AI build-out, and said costs will rise further in December and beyond, partly offset by product pricing. Apple has raised its memory purchase obligations by $33 billion from the June quarter.

The CFO guided to December-quarter revenue growth of 7% or more. The memory cost trend may matter for consumer electronics pricing more broadly as AI demand strains component supplies.

stories.headline: China Disputes Reports That Artillery Shell Was Found in Container in Papua New Guinea, Calls It a Wine Bottle
stories.summary:
China's embassy in Papua New Guinea has rejected reports that a suspected Chinese-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container, saying the object is a "shell-shaped wine bottle" that "poses no danger at all." Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was discovered at a construction site in the capital. Police commissioner David Manning called it "a very concerning discovery."

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation, citing unnamed sources, identified the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 artillery projectile containing chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this. Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that it was merely a dummy, according to the Post Courier.

The embassy said it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade shell to be smuggled out of China, citing the country's strict firearm laws. Some Facebook users were skeptical, asking what kind of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms and noting the object carried no labels. The case is notable given Papua New Guinea's strategic position and competing Chinese and Western influence in the Pacific. Authorities have not said what charges the four detainees face or whether the device has been confirmed live.

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Win Control of Both the Senate and House in Sweeping Midterm Results
stories.summary:
Democrats have taken control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, according to projections from the BBC's partner CBS News. CBS projected a Democratic House win shortly after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday), with the remaining question being the size of the majority as counting continues. The Senate results exceeded Democratic expectations, with pick-ups in North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine, and a hold in Michigan. One seat, in Alaska, remains a toss-up, and CBS reported that Mississippi was on a knife edge.

Several results stood out. Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932, and South Carolina had last done so in 1998. Texas shifted about nine points toward Democrats compared with the 2024 Senate race. In Florida, Democrats held two districts, 14 and 25, that Republicans had redrawn to favor Donald Trump voters, and also won the redrawn District 22, a blow to the Republican redistricting push.

A large exit poll suggested women turned out in large numbers and mostly voted Democratic, while men were evenly split. The economy was voters' top issue, followed by the state of democracy, and more than two-thirds said they believed Trump's policies had worsened economic conditions. Hispanic voters in Florida appeared to back the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon 55% to 44% over Republican Ashley Moody, reversing the roughly 55% Hispanic support Trump received in 2024.

National Review, a right-leaning outlet, described the outcome as an overwhelming rebuke of President Trump and Republicans, calling it an "Armageddon" election. The result shifts the balance of power in Washington for the second half of Trump's term, with Democrats now positioned to control committee gavels and legislative agendas in both chambers. Counting continues in the remaining contested races.

stories.headline: Democrat Annie Andrews Wins South Carolina Senate Seat, First Democratic Victory There in 28 Years
stories.summary:
Democrat Annie Andrews, a former pediatrician, is projected to have won South Carolina's Senate race, according to the BBC's US partner CBS. Her victory ends a 28-year Democratic drought in the state, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1998. Pre-election polling had rated the race as leaning Republican, and Donald Trump carried the state by 18 points in 2024.

Her opponent, Republican Darline Graham, was appointed in July after the sudden death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who had held the seat since 2002 and was one of Washington's most influential voices on foreign policy. Trump supported her appointment. A political newcomer, Graham acknowledged during the primary that she was "not that informed on national security."

Graham's campaign was dogged by questions about her inexperience. Asked in a recent debate about US policy toward Taiwan, she said: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

The South Carolina result was among the biggest upsets of a night in which Democrats gained ground across the Senate map. It contributed to a Democratic majority in the chamber, and reflects how far the political environment shifted from 2024 in states that Republicans had long considered safe.

stories.headline: Indonesia Arrests Former Police Chief Over Alleged Wiretapping of President Prabowo
stories.summary:
Indonesian authorities have arrested a former national police chief, Listyo, on allegations that he wiretapped the phones of President Prabowo Subianto and other top officials. A senior official said Wednesday that the conduct may amount to treason or an attempt to overthrow the government.

In response, Indonesia's military is mobilizing tens of thousands of troops to bolster security in Jakarta while investigators examine the alleged surveillance. The scale of the deployment points to official concern about possible instability in the capital.

The case is being reported by Bloomberg and Al Jazeera. Details of the evidence, the motive and the scope of the alleged wiretapping have not yet been made public. Further developments are expected as the investigation proceeds and prosecutors decide on formal charges.

stories.headline: Voters Approve Dozens of Data Center Moratoriums in Backlash Against AI Buildout
stories.summary:
Voters showed deep distrust of the artificial intelligence race on Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a number of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, according to Axios. The shift included Texas, described as the epicenter of the boom.

In an election that turned heavily on affordability concerns, voters appeared to view the AI expansion less as a technological advance and more as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities. Axios quoted one observer as saying, "What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake."

The results are a warning to technology companies and investors that local opposition to data center construction, tied to electricity costs and resource use, is becoming a political force. Further details on the specific measures and candidates were not available in the excerpt provided, and the long-term effect on planned projects remains to be seen.
